# A rank-two three-cap overlap inequality without original section stationarity

This is an ordinary continuous convex-body theorem and a scoped mixed-fiber
consequence. It does not establish the remaining cross-fiber inequality or
resolve (OC). In particular, the caps in the principal theorem need not be
stationary at the point where they are originally given.

## 1. Statement and constants

Let K be a convex body in R^d, d>=2, with volume V. Let H_1,H_2,H_3 be closed
halfspaces whose unit normals span a plane E, admit a strictly positive linear
dependence, and whose union is R^d. Write

    A_i = vol_d(K intersect H_i),
    O = A_1+A_2+A_3-V.

Thus O is the integral over K of the covering multiplicity minus one. Set

    c_2 = 4/9,                       r_2 = 3/4,
    b_d = max{4/3, sqrt(2(d-1)/d)},  c_d = 1/(1+b_d),
    r_d = 2-b_d                     (d>=3).

Then

    O >= r_d min_i A_i.                                      (1)

In every dimension 0<r_d<1 and c_d=1/(3-r_d). In particular r_d=2/3 for
3<=d<=9; for d>=10 it is strictly larger than 2-sqrt(2), and hence larger
than 1/2. Also c_d>=gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d. In d=2 the coefficient 3/4 in (1)
is sharp.

The statement also applies in the affine hull of any intrinsically
d-dimensional convex body, using its normalized intrinsic measure and the
restrictions of the three normals to that affine hull. The rank-two and
positive-circuit hypotheses are then hypotheses on those restrictions.

## 2. Precise continuous input: projected stationary sections

We use the following consequence of already proved ordinary convex geometry.

**Projected stationary-section lemma.** Let E be a two-dimensional subspace
of R^d, let 0 lie in the interior of the orthogonal projection of K to E,
and let u_i be unit vectors in E. Put

    S_i = H_(d-1)(K intersect {u_i.x=0}),
    p_i = vol_d(K intersect {u_i.x>=0})/V.

Suppose the projection to E of each section's centroid is 0. If theta_i>=0,
sum theta_i=1, and sum theta_i S_i u_i=0, then

    sum theta_i p_i >= c_d.                                 (2)

There is no hypothesis about the components of the section centroids in
E-perpendicular. Here and below proper sections have their usual positive
(d-1)-dimensional measure.

**Proof and exact dependencies.** Choose a point of int(K) whose projection
to E is 0, and translate K by its E-perpendicular component. This leaves all
the quantities and projected hypotheses unchanged and puts 0 in int(K).
Such an interior point exists: a linear map sends the interior of a
full-dimensional convex body onto the relative interior of its image. A
direct proof is to take a small simplex around the chosen projected point
inside the projection, lift its vertices to K, and mix their positive
barycentric combination slightly with an interior point of K while adjusting
the projected convex coefficients; the resulting lift is interior.

For d=2 this is the sharp planar centered-chord theorem proved in
`candidate c22519c29667168e`. Its normal balance is exactly
the hypothesis above, and it gives 4/9.

For d>=3 let

    f(x)=vol_(d-2)(K intersect (x+E-perpendicular)),  x in E.

Fiberwise Minkowski inclusion and Brunn--Minkowski make f^(1/(d-2)) concave
on its positive support; f(0)>0. Fubini identifies the p_i with the cap
fractions of f, and identifies S_i with the integral of f on the line
E intersect u_i-perpendicular. The projected section-centroid hypothesis
is exactly the assertion that each such line restriction has first moment
zero. No other component of a section's first moment occurs.

Form the planar Ball radial body B with

    rho_B(v)^2 = 2 integral_0^infinity t f(tv) dt.

Its convexity under these non-even hypotheses is proved in Lemma 2 of
`candidate 0f025bdf9a51573b`. Polar integration shows that it preserves
every through-origin cap fraction. The zero line first moments make the
corresponding chords of B centered. Let L_i be their lengths. The proved
centered-line comparison in
`candidate ceb2615ce03b7dbc` gives

    sqrt(d/[2(d-1)]) <= R_i:=S_i/[sqrt(f(0)) L_i] <= 1.

Put lambda_i=theta_i R_i/(sum_j theta_j R_j). Then
sum lambda_i L_i u_i=0. These are balanced chord weights, and the original
theta_i are their reweighting by factors q_i=1/R_i in [1,b_d]. The robust
planar reweighting theorem, Sections 1--4 of
`candidate 3ed6256a0896f434`, proves a cap mean
of at least 1/(1+b) for every b>=4/3 and q_i in [1,b]. Taking b=b_d proves
(2). This is also a verification that the proof of Section 5 of that source
uses only the projected centroid hypothesis, although its displayed
statement imposes the stronger full centroid hypothesis.

For 3<=d<=9, c_d=3/7>27/64=gamma_3>=gamma_d. For d>=10 we may weaken c_d
to 2/5, because b_d<3/2; then 2/5>gamma_6>=gamma_d. The integer comparison
for the strict inequality is 2*7^6=235298>233280=5*6^6. Finally gamma_d
decreases: the derivative of x log(x/(x+1)) is
-log(1+1/x)+1/(x+1)<0. This proves all stated constant comparisons. QED.

This lemma has explicit proved dependencies. It is not an invocation of a
mixed-integer theorem, nor of a rank-three stationary-section assertion.

## 3. Two elementary boundary and differentiability lemmas

**Halfplane boundary lemma.** If through-origin closed halfplanes cover a
plane, then at most two of them cover any prescribed closed halfplane G
through the origin.

To prove this, parameterize the interior directions of G by an open angular
interval of length pi. Each through-origin halfplane meets this interval
in an initial interval, a terminal interval, the whole interval, or the
empty set. A halfplane opposite to G may meet only its endpoint rays and
is empty on the open interval. If none contains the whole interval, retain
an initial interval reaching farthest and a terminal interval starting
earliest. They cover the open interval because the whole finite family
does. The corresponding closed halfplanes cover its two limiting endpoint
rays as well. This proves the assertion. Translations give the same result
for a common point y.

Consequently, if a convex planar set D lies in one closed halfplane through
y, then at most two members of a through-y halfplane cover of the plane
cover D. In particular this holds for y on the boundary of D or outside D,
by support or separation.

**Proper-cap first variation.** Fix a unit vector u and y such that the
hyperplane u.(x-y)=0 cuts int(K). Its cap volume is a C^1 function of the
normal and offset in a neighborhood of these parameters. Its derivatives
are

    gradient_y A = -S u,
    D_u A[v] = integral_section v.(x-y) dH_(d-1)(x),   v perpendicular u.
                                                               (3)

Here the first formula is restricted to allowed center directions if the
center is restricted to a subspace.

For a direct proof, choose coordinates u=e_d and write vertical fibers of
K as [a(x'),b(x')] over its compact projection. The cap cut by a nearby
hyperplane x_d=s+t.x' has volume

    integral [b(x')-max{a(x'),s+t.x'}]_+ dx'.

At a proper cut, the set where a(x')=s+t.x' or b(x')=s+t.x' has
(d-1)-measure zero: it is the boundary of the full-dimensional section in
that hyperplane, expressed in the x' coordinates. For clarity, every point
in the relative interior of a proper section is in int(K); otherwise a
supporting hyperplane to K at it would contain the whole section and hence
be the cutting hyperplane, contradicting properness. The displayed
integrand therefore has pointwise derivative
-1_{a<s+t.x'<b}(delta_s+delta_t.x') almost everywhere. Its difference
quotients are bounded by a fixed constant times |delta_s|+|delta_t| because
K is bounded. Dominated convergence gives the Frechet derivative and,
applied to these indicator formulas, its continuity. Translating from graph
coordinates to a unit normal gives (3), including the stated sign. This
argument needs no smoothness or strict convexity of K.

## 4. The concurrent-cap theorem by an attained variational minimum

Let D be the orthogonal projection of K to a fixed plane E. For y in D and
unit normals u_1,u_2,u_3 in E satisfying 0 in conv{u_1,u_2,u_3}, write

    A_i(y,u)=vol_d(K intersect {u_i.(x-y)>=0}),
    F_r(y,u)=sum_i A_i(y,u)-r min_i A_i(y,u),

where r=r_d. The caps cover the whole plane: otherwise all three scalar
products would be strictly negative, contradicting a convex dependence
giving 0.

The admissible parameter set is compact. The cap masses are continuous on
it by dominated convergence, since every hyperplane with nonzero normal
has d-volume zero. Thus F_r attains a minimum.

Whenever a pair of the caps covers K, say the pair other than i, we have

    F_r >= V+A_i-r min_j A_j >= V+(1-r)min_j A_j >= V.       (4)

If 0 lies on the boundary of the normal triangle, a pair of normals is
opposite, so its caps cover all space and (4) applies. If y lies on the
boundary of D, the halfplane boundary lemma again supplies a pair covering
D and hence K. The same argument proves F_r>=V at every y outside D.

Suppose, for contradiction, that the attained minimum is less than V. At
its parameters, y belongs to int(D) and 0 belongs to the interior of the
nondegenerate normal triangle. These are open conditions, so the two center
coordinates and the three normal angles are independent local variables.
All three cuts are proper: an interior point above y and a small ball
around it lie in K, and every normal lies in E. The first-variation lemma
therefore applies.

Write

    G_j=sum_i A_i-r A_j,              F_r=max_j G_j.

The active j are exactly the indices of minimum cap mass. At a local
minimum of a finite maximum of C^1 functions, zero lies in the convex hull
of its active gradients. Indeed, otherwise strict separation supplies a
direction along which every active function decreases; the inactive
functions have a fixed positive gap and remain below the former maximum
for a sufficiently small step. This contradicts local minimality.

It follows that there exist t_i>=0, sum t_i=1, supported on the minimum
caps, such that, putting alpha_i=1-r t_i,

    alpha_i >=1-r>0,   sum_i alpha_i=3-r,
    sum_i alpha_i gradient A_i=0.                         (5)

For each i only A_i depends on its own normal angle. That coordinate of
(5), with (3), forces the projection to E of the centroid of section i to
equal y: its component along u_i already equals u_i.y, and its component
in the perpendicular direction in E is fixed by the angle derivative.
The two center coordinates of (5) give

    sum_i alpha_i S_i u_i=0.                              (6)

The projected stationary-section lemma, translated by y in E and with
weights theta_i=alpha_i/(3-r), now yields

    F_r = sum_i alpha_i A_i
        >= (3-r)c_d V = V.                               (7)

Here the first equality uses the support of t_i on the minimum caps. This
contradicts the hypothetical minimum. We have proved F_r>=V for all
concurrent positive-circuit triples, including all degeneracies and all
locations of their concurrence point.

## 5. Removing concurrence and proving sharpness

Write the original caps as H_i={x:u_i.x>=b_i}, with u_i in E, and choose
lambda_i>0 with sum lambda_i=1 and sum lambda_i u_i=0. Put B=sum lambda_i b_i.
The linear map E -> R^3, x -> (u_i.x)_i, has image exactly the plane
lambda-perpendicular, since it has rank two. Hence there is a unique y in E
with

    u_i.y=b_i-B   for every i.                            (8)

The caps cover the plane if and only if B<=0. If B>0, (8) gives a point
strictly outside all three. Conversely, if B<=0, a point outside all three
would satisfy 0=sum lambda_i u_i.x < sum lambda_i b_i=B<=0, impossible.

Thus B<=0 in the present theorem, and the three caps through y,

    H_i'={x:u_i.x>=b_i-B},

are contained in the original caps and still cover the plane. The function
F_r(A)=sum A_i-r min A_i is coordinatewise nondecreasing when 0<=r<1:
increasing one coordinate by delta>=0 increases the sum by delta and the
minimum by at most delta. Section 4 consequently gives
F_r(A)>=F_r(A')>=V, exactly (1).

For sharpness in d=2 take any triangle and its three vertex caps whose
boundaries are parallel to the opposite sides and pass through its
centroid. In barycentric coordinates these caps are {ell_i>=1/3}, so they
cover the entire affine plane. Each has area 4V/9. Their excess is V/3,
and its ratio to the minimum cap area is 3/4. This verifies equality without
requiring any assertion about higher-dimensional sharpness.

All statements concern closed caps. Every proper cutting hyperplane has
zero d-volume, so no boundary mass has been lost in the variation or in
the multiplicity identity. After restricting to an intrinsic affine hull,
the same observation applies to the nonzero restricted normals in the
stated intrinsic version.

## 6. Exact mixed-fiber accounting, and the remaining inequality

Here is a consequence which uses the theorem on actual caps, without
requiring the original sections to have common centroids or profiles.
Suppose the measured positive fibers are partitioned into groups P_1,...,P_k.
For each group i there are three ambient caps H_(i,1),H_(i,2),H_(i,3).
Each has total mixed mass at most B. On every fiber z in P_i their
restrictions satisfy the rank-two positive-circuit plane-cover hypotheses
above in a common dimension d. Let V_z be its volume, and set

    a_(i,j)(z) = volume captured by H_(i,j) on fiber z,
    W_i = sum_(z in P_i) V_z,
    L_i = sum_(z in P_i) min_j a_(i,j)(z),
    X_i = sum_(j=1)^3 [mass captured by H_(i,j) outside P_i].

Applying (1) separately to every owned fiber gives the exact inequality

    3B >= W_i+r_d L_i+X_i.                               (9)

Every one of the three global cap masses is at least L_i, so
Delta_i:=B-L_i>=0. On summing (9), and writing M=sum_i W_i, we obtain

    (3-r_d) k B >= M+sum_i X_i-r_d sum_i Delta_i.          (10)

Thus the additional, presently unproved condition

    sum_i X_i >= r_d sum_i Delta_i                       (11)

would imply B>=c_d M/k>=gamma_d M/k for this configuration. No claim that
(11) holds for arbitrary mixed-integer covers is made here. In particular,
neither cardinality nor this local overlap theorem alone supplies its sign.

The simplex product calibrates (9)--(10) in d=2 with one isolated fiber per
group and the three canonical triangle caps: then L_i=B, X_i=Delta_i=0,
and equality holds. At the nonstationary planar triangle example with cap
fractions 9/25,12/25,12/25, the excess is 8/25 and its ratio to the minimum
is 8/9>3/4, consistent with (1); the false uniform bound O>=V/3 is not used.
If a circuit has zero overlap on a fiber and one zero local cap, (1) gives
zero additional charge there, as it must. These checks distinguish (1)
from the previously falsified positive-charge and constant-profile claims.

## 7. Scope and dependency graph

The proof uses proper-cap differentiation and a compact variational problem;
it makes no assertion about unattained mixed-depth optima. Its continuous
dependencies are the proved planar centered-chord theorem, the proved
non-even Ball radial-body convexity lemma, the proved centered-line
comparison, and the proved robust planar reweighting theorem. The only new
use of these dependencies is at the attained variational minimum.

For three arbitrary normals in a higher-dimensional space, a positive
dependence already forces rank at most two; the theorem above handles the
genuine rank-two case. It does not handle larger positive circuits of rank
three or more, or establish the cross-fiber credit (11). It is therefore a
new local continuous input, not a resolution of (OC).
